figures.shows: Six heat maps of cosine similarity between character n-grams of a vocabulary word (y axis) and of an out-of-vocabulary word (x axis): rarity-scarceness, young-preadolescent, paving-asphaltic, chip-microcircuit, connect-interlink, spiciness-piquancy. Red is positive cosine, blue negative; the colour bar has no numbers. Visible blocks: the suffix n-grams of rarity (-ity) and scarceness (-ness) are strongly red; chip n-grams match a group of micro and circuit n-grams; paving matches the asphalt n-grams.

papers.what_it_is: A 2017 Facebook AI Research paper that extends the skipgram word-embedding model so that each word vector is the sum of vectors of its character n-grams (fastText), and evaluates it on similarity, analogy and language modeling tasks in nine languages.

assertions.value: The authors propose an approach based on the skipgram model in which each word is represented as a bag of character n-grams, with a vector for each n-gram and the word represented as the sum of these vectors.
quotes: we propose a new approach based on the skipgram model, where each word is represented as a bag of character n-grams.
A vector representation is associated to each character n-gram; words being represented as the sum of these representations.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own model; Section 3.2 defines it.

assertions.value: The authors state that their main contribution is an extension of the continuous skipgram model that takes subword information into account.
quotes: Our main contribution is to introduce an extension of the continuous skipgram model (Mikolov et al., 2013b), which takes into account subword information.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the scope of their own contribution (Section 1).

assertions.value: The authors state that most word-representation techniques give each word a distinct vector without parameter sharing and so ignore the internal structure of words, which they call an important limitation for morphologically rich languages such as Turkish or Finnish.
quotes: Most of these techniques represent each word of the vocabulary by a distinct vector, without parameter sharing.
they ignore the internal structure of words, which is an important limitation for morphologically rich languages, such as Turkish or Finnish.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement with no evidence in the paper at this point.

assertions.value: The authors state that in French or Spanish most verbs have more than forty different inflected forms, while Finnish has fifteen cases for nouns.
quotes: in French or Spanish, most verbs have more than forty different inﬂected forms, while the Finnish language has ﬁfteen cases for nouns.
assertions.certainty_reason: A linguistic statement given without a citation.

assertions.value: The authors state that languages with many word forms that occur rarely or not at all in the training corpus make it difficult to learn good word representations, and that because many word formations follow rules, character-level information can improve vectors for morphologically rich languages.
quotes: making it difﬁcult to learn good word representations.
it is possible to improve vector representations for morphologically rich languages by using character level information.
assertions.certainty_reason: The motivation is an author claim; later sections test it.

assertions.value: The authors state that earlier composition-function approaches rely on a morphological decomposition of words, while their approach does not.
quotes: These different approaches rely on a morphological decomposition of words, while ours does not.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state what their own method does and does not use (Section 2).

assertions.value: The authors attribute to Schutze (1993) the learning of representations of character four-grams through singular value decomposition, with word representations derived by summing the four-gram representations.
quotes: Closest to our approach, Schütze (1993) learned representations of character four-grams through singular value decomposition, and derived representations for words by summing the four-grams representations.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that Wieting et al. (2016) also represent words with character n-gram count vectors, but learn them with an objective based on paraphrase pairs, while the authors' model can be trained on any text corpus.
quotes: Wieting et al. (2016) also proposed to represent words using character n-gram count vectors.
the objective function used to learn these representations is based on paraphrase pairs, while our model can be trained on any text corpus.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of other work, plus an author claim about their own model.

assertions.value: The authors review the continuous skipgram model: given a corpus as a sequence of words, the objective is to maximize a log-likelihood of the context words of each word, where the context is the set of indices of words surrounding that word.
quotes: the objective of the skipgram model is to maximize the following log-likelihood:
where the context Ct is the set of indices of words surrounding word wt.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the objective it builds on as a definition in Section 3.1.
assertions.reader_inference: The formula itself is lost in the text layer; only the prose statement is quoted.

assertions.value: The authors frame the prediction of context words as a set of independent binary classification tasks: context words are positive examples, negatives are sampled at random from the dictionary, and the binary logistic loss is used.
quotes: The problem of predicting context words can instead be framed as a set of independent binary classiﬁcation tasks.
we consider all context words as positive examples and sample negatives at random from the dictionary.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the training setup it uses (Section 3.1).

assertions.value: The authors parameterize the skipgram score between a word and a context word as the scalar product of the word's input vector and the context word's output vector, and state that this is the skipgram model with negative sampling of Mikolov et al.
quotes: Then the score can be computed as the scalar product between word and context vectors as s(wt, wc) = uwtvwc.
The model described in this section is the skipgram model with negative
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the baseline score function in Section 3.1.

assertions.value: The authors represent each word as a bag of character n-grams and score a word against a context word by the sum, over the n-grams of the word, of the n-gram vector times the context vector.
quotes: Each word w is represented as a bag of character n-gram.
We represent a word by the sum of the vector representations of its n-grams.
We thus obtain the scoring function:
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its scoring function in Section 3.2.

assertions.value: The authors add the special boundary symbols < and > at the beginning and end of each word, which allows distinguishing prefixes and suffixes from other character sequences.
quotes: We add special boundary symbols < and > at the beginning and end of words, allowing to distinguish preﬁxes and sufﬁxes from other character sequences.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own preprocessing (Section 3.2).

assertions.value: The authors also include the word itself in the set of its n-grams, to learn a representation for each word in addition to the character n-grams, and note that the sequence for the word her differs from the tri-gram her inside the word where.
quotes: We also include the word w itself in the set of its n-grams, to learn a representation for each word (in addition to character n-grams).
Note that the sequence <her>, corresponding to the word her is different from the tri-gram her from the word where.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own representation (Section 3.2).

assertions.value: The authors extract all n-grams with n from 3 to 6, and state that this is a very simple approach and that different sets of n-grams could be considered, for example all prefixes and suffixes.
quotes: In practice, we extract all the n-grams for n greater or equal to 3 and smaller or equal to 6.
This is a very simple approach, and different sets of n-grams could be considered, for example taking all preﬁxes and sufﬁxes.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own n-gram range (Section 3.2); Section 5.5 tests other ranges.

assertions.value: The authors state that summing n-gram vectors allows sharing representations across words, and so allows learning reliable representations for rare words.
quotes: This simple model allows sharing the representations across words, thus allowing to learn reliable representation for rare words.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim at the point it is made; Sections 5.1 and 5.4 give the supporting results.

assertions.value: The authors bound the memory of the model by hashing n-grams to integers in 1 to K with the Fowler-Noll-Vo hashing function (the FNV-1a variant); a word is then represented by its index in the word dictionary and the set of hashed n-grams it contains.
quotes: we use a hashing function that maps n-grams to integers in 1 to K.
We hash character sequences using the Fowler-Noll-Vo hashing function (speciﬁcally the FNV-1a variant).
Ultimately, a word is represented by its index in the word dictionary and the set of hashed n-grams it contains.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own implementation choice (Section 3.2).

assertions.value: The authors set K = 2.106 as the text layer prints it.
quotes: We set K = 2.106 below.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setting (Section 3.2).
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer flattened an exponent; the value is probably 2 times 10 to the sixth, about two million hash buckets. The PDF page was not rendered to confirm.

assertions.value: The authors compare their model in most experiments to the C implementation of the skipgram and cbow models from the word2vec package, except in the comparison of Section 5.3.
quotes: In most experiments (except in Sec. 5.3), we compare our model to the C implementation
of the skipgram and cbow models from the word2vec2 package.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own baseline (Section 4.1).

assertions.value: The authors optimize with stochastic gradient descent with a linear decay of the step size, carried out in parallel with Hogwild, with all threads sharing parameters and updating vectors asynchronously.
quotes: we use a linear decay of the step size.
All threads share parameters and update vectors in an asynchronous manner.
in parallel, by resorting to Hogwild
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own training procedure (Section 4.2).

assertions.value: The authors use word vectors of dimension 300 for both their model and the baselines.
quotes: the word vectors have dimension 300.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setting (Section 4.3).

assertions.value: The authors sample 5 negatives for each positive example, at random with probability proportional to the square root of the unigram frequency.
quotes: For each positive example, we sample 5 negatives at random, with probability proportional to the square root of the uni-gram frequency.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setting (Section 4.3).

assertions.value: The authors use a context window of size c, with c sampled uniformly between 1 and 5.
quotes: We use a context window of size c, and uniformly sample the size c between 1 and 5.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setting (Section 4.3).

assertions.value: The authors subsample the most frequent words with a rejection threshold of 10-4, as printed in the text layer.
quotes: In order to subsample the most frequent words, we use a rejection threshold of 10−4
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setting (Section 4.3).

assertions.value: The authors keep, when building the word dictionary, the words that appear at least 5 times in the training set.
quotes: we keep the words that appear at least 5 times in the training set.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setting (Section 4.3).

assertions.value: The authors set the initial step size to 0.025 for the skipgram baseline and to 0.05 for both their model and the cbow baseline.
quotes: The step size γ0 is set to 0.025 for the skipgram baseline and to 0.05 for both our model and the cbow baseline.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setting (Section 4.3).

assertions.value: The authors state that these step sizes are the default values in the word2vec package and work well for their model too.
quotes: These are the default values in the word2vec package and work well for our model too.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement with no tuning experiment reported.

assertions.value: On English data the authors report that their model with character n-grams is approximately 1.5x slower to train than the skipgram baseline, processing 105k words per second per thread against 145k for the baseline.
quotes: our model with character n-grams is approximately 1.5× slower to train than the skipgram baseline.
we process 105k words/second/thread versus 145k words/second/thread for the baseline.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single timing measurement on one setup; hardware is not stated.
assertions.reader_inference: The 145k/105k ratio is about 1.4, close to the stated 1.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that their model is implemented in C++ and is publicly available.
quotes: Our model is implemented in C++, and is publicly available.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own implementation (Section 4.3).

assertions.value: The authors train on Wikipedia dumps in nine languages: Arabic, Czech, German, English, Spanish, French, Italian, Romanian and Russian, except in the comparison to previous work of Section 5.3.
quotes: Except for the comparison to previous work (Sec. 5.3), we train our models on Wikipedia data.
We downloaded Wikipedia dumps in nine languages: Arabic, Czech, German, English,
Spanish, French, Italian, Romanian and Russian.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own training data (Section 4.4).

assertions.value: The authors shuffle all the datasets and train their models with five passes over them.
quotes: All the datasets are shufﬂed, and we train our models by doing ﬁve passes over them.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own training setting (Section 4.4).

assertions.value: The authors evaluate word similarity by computing Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between human judgement and the cosine similarity between the vector representations.
quotes: between human judgement and the cosine similarity between the vector representations.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own evaluation protocol (Section 5.1).

assertions.value: The authors evaluate German on the datasets GUR65, GUR350 and ZG222 and Russian on the HJ dataset.
quotes: For German, we compare the different models on three datasets: GUR65, GUR350 and ZG222
Russian word vectors are evaluated using the HJ dataset introduced by Panchenko et al. (2016).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own evaluation datasets (Section 5.1).

assertions.value: The authors represent evaluation words that are absent from the training data with null vectors by default (called sisg-), and with the sum of the word's n-gram vectors in the variant called sisg.
quotes: we propose by default to use null vectors for these words.
We do so by taking the sum of its n-gram vectors.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines sisg- and sisg in Section 5.1.

assertions.value: The authors report that the sisg model outperforms the baselines on all word similarity datasets except the English WS353 dataset.
quotes: First, by looking at Table 1, we notice that the proposed model (sisg), which uses subword information, outperforms the baselines on all datasets except the English WS353 dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; Table 1 reports single scores with no variance.
assertions.reader_inference: In Table 1 (viewed) sisg ties sisg- at 81 on DE GUR65 and ties sg and sisg- at 75 on FR RG65 only against sg; the claim holds for the cells shown. No seeds or significance tests are reported.

assertions.value: The authors report that computing vectors for out-of-vocabulary words (sisg) is always at least as good as not doing so (sisg-).
quotes: computing vectors for out-of-vocabulary words (sisg) is always at least as good as not doing so (sisg-).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Table 1 results prove the advantage of using subword information in the form of character n-grams.
quotes: This proves the advantage of using subword information in the form of character n-grams.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author interpretation of empirical results; the paper gives no proof.
assertions.reader_inference: Single-run correlations on small evaluation sets support, but do not prove, the claim.

assertions.value: The authors report that the effect of using character n-grams is more important for Arabic, German and Russian than for English, French or Spanish.

assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.certainty_reason: A linguistic statement given without a citation.

assertions.value: The authors state that many German words are compound words, and that character-level similarity between Tischtennis and Tennis keeps the model from treating the two words as completely different.
